html:
An earthen dam across the Wadi Adhanah near Marib, the capital of the kingdom of Saba in what is now Yemen. Begun in the 8th century BCE, it caught the seasonal floods off the mountains and sent them through canals to a large oasis, the base of Saba's wealth along with the incense trade.

The dam was raised and repaired many times over more than a thousand years, the last great repairs by kings of the Himyarite Kingdom in the 5th and 6th centuries CE. Inscriptions record the labour of thousands of workers.

It finally broke for good in the late 500s CE, and the oasis returned to desert. The Quran tells of the "flood of the dam" as a punishment on the people of Saba. Arab tradition links the collapse to the migration of tribes from south Arabia to the north, among them the ancestors of the Ghassanids and of the Aws and Khazraj of Medina. A new dam was built near the site in 1986.
